find: Innocent Smoothies is a classic UK example. Three Cambridge graduates started it in 1999 with £500 of fruit. They grew via small business loans and, years later, crowdfunded rounds and a share sale to Coca-Cola. Early on they had no trading history — a bank would not lend them six-figure sums, so they relied on a mix of owner’s savings and family support. As the business grew, it could access loans, new share issues and eventually sell a stake to a global giant.
replace: Innocent Smoothies is a classic UK example. Three Cambridge graduates spent £500 of their own money on fruit and sold smoothies from a stall at a London music festival in 1998, then set the business up the year after. With no trading history, they could not raise the sums they needed from a bank. The breakthrough was a private investor, Maurice Pinto, who put in £250,000 in return for a stake — equity, not a loan. Coca-Cola then bought a minority stake for £30 million in 2009 and took majority control in 2010.
note: F1: the crowdfunded rounds, the early small business loans and the family support are invented. Innocent struggled to raise money until Maurice Pinto invested £250,000 for a stake; Coca-Cola bought about 18% for £30m in April 2009 and 58% in April 2010. The £500 of fruit and the festival were 1998.

find: Innocent Smoothies started with savings, grew via loans, then used share issues.
replace: Innocent Smoothies started with the founders’ own £500, then grew by selling a stake to an outside investor.
note: F2: Innocent did not grow via loans. The growth finance was equity sold to a private investor, then stakes sold to Coca-Cola.

find: AQA will not give you the formulae for break-even or ARR — memorise them. For break-even questions, always calculate contribution per unit first, then divide fixed costs by that figure.
replace: AQA does not give you formulae in the exam, so learn the ARR formula by heart. Break-even is different: you are asked to read the break-even output and the margin of safety off a break-even chart, not to use the break-even formula. Practise finding the point where the total revenue line crosses the total cost line, then measuring across to actual output.

find: Supermarkets typically run net margins of 2-5%. Luxury brands like Burberry run 15-20%. Context decides whether a number is good or bad.
replace: Supermarkets typically run net margins of 2-5%: tiny mark-ups on huge volumes. Luxury brands charge far bigger mark-ups, so their gross margins are much higher — but a high gross margin does not guarantee a high net margin. In the year to March 2026 Burberry made £20 million of net profit on £2,420 million of sales, a net margin under 1%. Context decides whether a number is good or bad.
note: F14: Burberry's net margin is about 0.8%, not 15-20% (FY to 28 March 2026: revenue £2,420m, operating income £115m, net income £20m). The corrected version also makes the gross-versus-net point the lesson is teaching.
